segments.english: The LORD appeared to him at the terebinths of Mamre while he was sitting at the entrance of the tent in the heat of the day.
segments.literal: and-appeared to-him the-LORD in-terebinths-of Mamre and-he sitting at-entrance-of the-tent like-heat-of the-day

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of the niphal of ra'ah; the sequential narrative form 'and he appeared'.
YHWH, rendered LORD in capitals (decisions: divine names).
construct state: 'the terebinths of'.
A man's name (BDB: n.pr.m), as at 14:13, 'Mamre the Amorite'; the terebinths are his. Rashi: in his portion. See the commentary.
the conjunction and pronoun together open a circumstantial clause.
qal active participle, masculine singular.
construct state: 'the entrance of'.
construct state: 'the heat of'. The kaf is temporal, 'at about': the middle of the day.

phrases.literal: 'and-appeared to-him the-LORD': the verb comes first in the Hebrew, so the subject comes first in the English.
'in-terebinths-of Mamre': the preposition bet with the construct, here locating the scene.
'and-he sitting': the conjunction and the participle give the background to the appearance.

phrases.english: at the entrance of the tent
phrases.literal: 'at-entrance-of the-tent': the construct chain; the English 'at' is supplied.

phrases.english: in the heat of the day
phrases.literal: 'like-heat-of the-day': kaf of time, 'about the time of' the day's heat, i.e. the hottest part of the day; the English 'in the heat of the day' carries it.

grammar: The verb is wayyiqtol (the narrative sequential form). Here it is niphal: the English 'appeared' is the stem's sense 'appear, be seen'.
The clause 'while he was sitting' is circumstantial: the Hebrew joins a participle to the pronoun, which marks a background situation rather than a second action.
Construct chains: 'the entrance of the tent' and 'the heat of the day'. Both are read as single English noun phrases.
The etnahta on Mamre (18:1.5) divides the verse. The first part places the scene at the terebinths of Mamre; the second describes Abraham sitting at the tent in the heat.
segments.note: The divine name is written YHWH in the Hebrew; the English is 'the LORD' per the decisions.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the LORD appeared to him 'to visit the sick' (לְבַקֵּר אֶת הַחוֹלֶה): it was the third day after his circumcision, and the Holy One came to ask after his welfare (Bava Metzia 86b). Rashi gives the purpose of the appearance, not a sense of the verb; the English 'appeared' stands.

Ibn Ezra: some say the Name and the three men are one and the same and cannot be divided; they forgot 'the two angels came to Sodom' (19:1). Other interpreters say the Name appeared to Abraham in prophetic vision, and afterwards he lifted his eyes and saw three angels: one to bring the news to Sarah, two to Sodom, one to destroy and one to save Lot. The English keeps 'The LORD appeared' and then 'three men'.

Rashi: Mamre is the man who gave Abraham counsel about the circumcision; therefore God revealed Himself to Abraham in Mamre's portion (Bereshit Rabba). 'The terebinths of Mamre' are the grove that belongs to Mamre, the Amorite of 14:13, and the English agrees with this.

Rashi: the word is written ישב without a vav, so it can be read יָשַׁב 'he sat': Abraham wanted to stand, and the Holy One said to him, 'Sit, and I will stand'. This is a sign for his children that God will stand among the judges while they sit (Ps. 82:1). A homily; the English keeps the participle 'sitting'.
Rashi: he sat at the entrance to watch for passers-by and bring them into his house. This gives the purpose, not the sense of the words.

Rashi: the LORD brought out the sun from its sheath so as not to trouble Abraham with guests; seeing him grieve that no guests came, He sent the angels in the form of men. A homily on the heat of the day.

Ibn Ezra glosses 'and they ate' (18:8) as 'the bread was consumed', like 'which the fire consumes' (Lev. 6:3): not that the visitors ate as men eat. The comment is filed at 18:1 but bears on 18:8. The English keeps 'they ate'; see the note and the apparatus on 18:8.

Radak: the LORD appeared where Abraham lived (14:13), after the circumcision, to make Sodom's fate known to him, since Abraham was the greatest man of his generation. He allows that the whole account to 18:33 was a prophetic vision, begun while Abraham sat at the tent door. The English reads a narrated event and records the vision reading.

apparatus: Ramban: the appearance is honour and reward for the circumcision (not a message). Radak: it came after the circumcision to tell Abraham of Sodom, and he allows that the whole account to 18:33 was a prophetic vision. Neither is adopted as the plain reading of the narrative; both are recorded.
Ibn Ezra reads the three 'men' as angels in human form (see his comment on 18:1); the Hebrew calls them אֲנָשִׁים, and the English keeps 'men'.
context: אֵלוֹן is a large, long-lived tree, usually rendered terebinth or oak; the exact species is uncertain. Prominent trees were landmarks and places of meeting, judging and worship in Canaan, and the narrative names this camp by its trees (see also 13:18, 14:13).
Abraham lives as a herder in a tent. Resting in the shade at the tent entrance in the middle of the day is the ordinary habit of a household in a hot country.
Mamre is a place near Hebron (13:18); the same word names a man, an Amorite ally of Abraham (14:13, 24). Rashi takes the name here as that man; the English takes the place.

segments.english: He lifted his eyes and saw, and look, three men were standing before him. When he saw them, he ran from the entrance of the tent to meet them, and bowed down to the ground.
segments.literal: and-lifted his-eyes and-saw and-look three men standing upon-him and-saw and-ran to-meet-them from-entrance-of the-tent and-bowed-down to-the-ground

tokens.note: dual with a 3ms suffix: 'his eyes'. 'Lift the eyes' (נשׂא עינים) is an idiom for looking up or looking intently.
wayyiqtol, the first seeing.
hinneh: 'look' (not 'behold').
niphal participle, plural.

literally 'upon him'. With the participle of נצב it means standing at someone's side or in attendance on him (Ruth 2:5; Gen 45:1). Rashi: 'before him'; Ramban: facing him, watching; Radak and Sforno: waiting on him, to speak with him.

the second wayyar of the verse, a resumptive 'seeing': Ramban and Radak take it as seeing them again or seeing them stand and not move on; Rashi reads it as 'understood' (his midrash adds the bandage). The English keeps the plain verb.
wayyiqtol.
infinitive construct with the 3mp suffix.
the preposition min with the construct.
wayyiqtol of the hitpa'el: 'bow down, prostrate oneself'.
directional he on the noun: 'to the ground'.

phrases.english: He lifted his eyes and saw
phrases.literal: 'and-lifted his-eyes and-saw': the idiom 'lift the eyes' is literal; the first two wayyiqtols of the sequence.

phrases.english: and look, three men were standing before him
phrases.literal: 'and-look three men standing upon-him': hinneh introduces what he saw; 'upon him' with the participle 'standing' is read as standing at his side or in front of him, in attendance.
'and-saw': the second וַיַּרְא repeats the verb and resumes the narrative before Abraham's response; Rashi reads 'understood', Radak 'again'.

phrases.english: he ran from the entrance of the tent to meet them
phrases.literal: 'and-ran to-meet-them from-entrance-of the-tent': the English moves the 'from' phrase before the infinitive.

phrases.english: and bowed down to the ground
phrases.literal: 'and-bowed-down to-the-ground': the reflexive stem with the directional ending.

grammar: The verbs form a chain: he lifted, he saw, (he saw), he ran, he bowed. The second וַיַּרְא resumes the narrative, 'when he saw them', and is the turning point from sight to action.
הִנֵּה introduces what Abraham sees and draws the reader into his view: 'and look, three men'.
נִצָּבִים is a niphal participle, masculine plural, agreeing with 'men'; with עָלָיו it means standing at his side or in front of him, in attendance.

לִקְרָאתָם is lamed with the infinitive construct of קרא 'meet' and a 3mp suffix: 'to meet them'. וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ is the short wayyiqtol of the reflexive stem of שחה, 'bow down'; אָרְצָה carries the directional ending.
segments.note: The second וַיַּרְא is read as 'again' (Radak), as 'saw that they stood there' (Ramban) or as 'understood' (Rashi). The English 'When he saw them' keeps the plain verb. The Hebrew calls them אֲנָשִׁים; Ibn Ezra takes them to be angels (see 18:1), and the English keeps 'men'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the three are three messengers with three tasks (one to tell Sarah, one to overturn Sodom, one to heal Abraham), since one angel does not do two missions; the text uses the plural throughout (they ate, they said). Midrash on the purpose of the visitors. Ibn Ezra gives other tasks (one to announce, one to destroy, one to save Lot). The English keeps 'three men'.
Rashi: 'standing upon him' means 'standing before him'; it is a courteous expression used of the angels.

Rashi: the first 'saw' is literal; the second is 'understanding': he looked, saw them standing in one place and understood that they did not want to trouble him; though they knew he would come out to them, they waited out of respect, and he ran ahead to meet them. The Talmud (Bava Metzia 86b) adds that they withdrew when they saw him loosing and tying his bandage, at which he ran to them. The English 'When he saw them' keeps the plain verb.
Radak: the second 'and saw' means 'another time', that he saw them again. The English does not adopt it.

Radak: 'standing upon him' means standing near him, in attendance for his benefit or to meet his wish, as in 1 Sam. 22:7, unlike Gen. 28:13. Abraham saw them standing and not going on, as if waiting for him to call them, and ran to meet them. The English 'before him' keeps the sense of attendance.

context: The visitors are called 'men' (אֲנָשִׁים). The narrator has just said that the LORD appeared; Ibn Ezra takes the three men to be angels in human form, and 19:1 calls two of them angels. The text does not say that Abraham knew who they were.

To bow to the ground (hishtaḥavah) was the ordinary gesture of respect to a superior or honoured stranger across the ancient Near East. The verb is also used of worship; the context decides, and here it is the courtesy of a host.

segments.english: He said, "My lord, if I have found favour in your sight, please do not pass by your servant."
segments.literal: and-said my-lord if now I-found favour in-your-eyes not now pass-over from-upon your-servant

tokens.note: a plural noun ('lords') with the 1cs suffix, pointed with qamats: אֲדֹנָי. The qamats pointing is the one the tradition uses for God, but the word can be an honorific plural of respect for a person. The verbs addressed to him are singular. See the apparatus.
the particle na (entreaty), which the English carries as 'please' in the second place.
qatal, 1cs.
idiom: 'in your eyes' means 'in your sight'.
negative 'al, with the jussive that follows.
the second na.
qal jussive, 2ms: a negative command.
'from upon': with 'pass by', the preposition gives the sense 'pass by from the side of'.
'thy servant, I': a humble self-reference, 'I, your servant'.

phrases.literal: 'and-said': the wayyiqtol introduces the speech.
'my-lord': the form is treated as singular in the English, following Rashi.

phrases.english: if I have found favour in your sight
phrases.literal: 'if now I-found favour in-your-eyes': a conditional with a qatal; the particle na is carried by the 'please' that follows.

phrases.english: please do not pass by your servant
phrases.literal: 'not now pass-over from-upon your-servant': a negative request; the particle na comes before the verb.

grammar: The condition (protasis) 'if I have found favour' leads to the request, a negative jussive: 'do not pass on'. The conditional clause often opens a polite request.
אִם־נָא 'if now': נָא softens the condition into a courteous request. The second נָא in אַל־נָא makes the prohibition an entreaty, rendered 'please'.
'Your servant' (עַבְדֶּךָ) is the speaker's self-reference: 'I, your servant' (the pack lists this as sense 6). It is the usual courteous form before a superior.
מֵעַל עַבְדֶּךָ 'from upon your servant' with the verb 'pass': 'do not pass on from me'. The silluq ends the verse; the tipḥa on 'pass' sets 'do not pass' apart from 'from your servant'.
segments.note: אֲדֹנָי with qamats may address God or a person. The English 'my lord' (lower case) is the reading consistent with Ibn Ezra's view that the three are angels in human form (his comment on 18:1; the pack has no comment of his on this word). Rashi's second view and Radak's second, that Abraham addresses the LORD, is recorded in the apparatus.

commentary.summary: Rashi: Abraham spoke to the greatest of the three but called them all 'lords' (אֲדוֹנִים); he asked the greatest not to pass by, since if he stayed his companions would stay with him. In this reading the word is profane (Shevuot 35b). Another reading: the word is holy, and Abraham asked the Holy One to wait for him while he ran and brought in the guests; the words were said before 'he ran to meet them', though written after. Both readings are in Bereshit Rabba. The English keeps the singular address 'My lord' to the greatest of them; Rashi's plural 'lords' and his holy reading are recorded.

Radak: the rabbis differ. Some say the word is secular and Abraham spoke to the greatest of the three angels, who rank above one another; he said אֲדֹנָי with qamats out of respect, as Gideon did to an angel (Judg. 6:15). Others say it is holy and Abraham spoke to the LORD, asking Him to wait; from this they learned that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Presence. The English follows the first view and records the second.

apparatus: אֲדֹנָי with qamats: Rashi, second view (Shevuot 35b), and Radak, second view: the word is a name of God, and Abraham asked the LORD to wait while he welcomed the guests. Not adopted: the English addresses the visitors.

Rashi, first view and Radak: Abraham spoke to the greatest of the three. Ramban: he spoke to each of the three in turn, urging each. The singular verbs do not decide between these; the English leaves it open.
context: To 'find favour in someone's eyes' is the ordinary polite formula for asking a superior's goodwill, and 'your servant' the ordinary self-designation of a speaker before a superior; neither describes Abraham's actual standing.
The form אֲדֹנָי with qamats is the one the tradition reads as divine; the commentators disagree whether Abraham addresses the LORD or the visitors (see the apparatus).

segments.english: "Please, let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree."
segments.literal: let-be-brought please little-of water and-wash your-feet and-rest-yourselves under the-tree

tokens.note: Qal passive jussive, 3ms: 'let it be taken/brought'. The entry lists this passive under Pu 1 ('be taken'); the stem makes the agent unnamed: Radak, 'by one of the servants'.
particle na of entreaty.
construct of me'at, 'a little'.
qal imperative, 2mp.
dual with a 2mp suffix; 'your feet'.
nifal imperative, 2mp; the sense 'lean, rest' follows the context.

phrases.english: Please let a little water be brought
phrases.literal: 'let-be-brought please little-of water': the passive jussive, the particle, then the object.
'and-wash your-feet': the imperative with the conjunction.

phrases.english: and rest yourselves under the tree
phrases.literal: 'and-rest-yourselves under the-tree'.

grammar: The passive jussive 'let [water] be brought' has no stated agent. Rashi takes it that a servant brings it.
The imperatives (wash, rest) are in the plural; they address the three men together.
The etnahta on feet (18:4.6) divides the verse: the water and washing first, the resting place second.
The construct me'at-mayim: 'a little of water', a quantity phrase.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the passive 'let be brought' means through an agent, a servant, just as the LORD paid Israel through an agent (Num. 20:11, where Moses struck the rock). The English keeps the passive, which leaves the agent unstated.

Rashi: Abraham took them for Arabs who bow down to the dust of their feet, and so was careful not to bring idolatry into his house. Lot, who was not careful, gave lodging before washing (Gen. 19:2). A reason for the request, not a reading of the words.
Rashi: 'under the tree' means under the ilan, the tree. The English 'under the tree' follows.

context: Travellers went on foot, in sandals or barefoot, over dusty tracks; the host's first courtesy was water for the feet, often through a servant (compare 19:2, 24:32, 43:24).
The shade of a large tree in the heat of the day is offered as a place to rest, not as lodging.

segments.english: "Let me fetch a morsel of bread, and sustain your hearts; afterward you may go on, since you have passed by your servant." They said, "Do so, as you have said."
segments.literal: and-let-me-fetch a-morsel-of bread and-sustain your-hearts after you-will-pass-on for on-this-account you-passed upon your-servant and-they-said so you-do as-you-spoke

tokens.note: cohortative, 1cs: 'let me fetch'.
construct of pat, 'a morsel'.
imperative, 2mp. The verb is 'support'; the sense 'sustain' follows the phrase.
the heart as the seat of the appetites: 'sustain your hearts' means 'refresh yourselves' with food. Rashi notes the spelling לִבְּכֶם, not לְבַבְכֶם.
yiqtol, 2mp: a future, here a permission or a polite instruction.
the conjunction ki al-ken: 'since, for this reason'.
part of the conjunction ki al-ken.
part of the conjunction ki al-ken.
qatal, 2mp.
singular servant with a 2mp suffix: 'your servant', addressing the three together.
wayyiqtol, 3mp.
adverb of manner.
yiqtol, 2ms: the speech turns to Abraham in the singular.
piel qatal, 2ms.

phrases.english: Let me fetch a morsel of bread
phrases.literal: 'and-let-me-fetch a-morsel-of bread'.
'and-sustain your-hearts': see the commentary on the bread that sustains the heart.
'after you-will-pass-on': the English puts the future in the permissive.
'for on-this-account you-passed': the compound conjunction gives the reason.
'upon your-servant': the preposition 'al with the 2mp suffix on servant.

phrases.english: They said, "Do so, as you have said."
phrases.literal: 'and-they-said so you-do as-you-spoke': the reply, in the singular to Abraham.

grammar: The speech has two parts: Abraham's offer (a cohortative, 'let me fetch', then an imperative, 'sustain', then a yiqtol of permission, 'you may go on') and the visitors' reply.
The compound כִּי־עַל־כֵּן: 'since, for this reason'. Ibn Ezra: it means 'since' (הואיל), as in 19:8. The qatal 'you have passed' is the reason clause.
The visitors speak as a group (plural verb, 'they said') but answer Abraham in the singular (תַּעֲשֶׂה, דִּבַּרְתָּ). The yiqtol תַּעֲשֶׂה 'you do' has the force of a polite command.
The etnaḥta on עַבְדְּכֶם divides the verse: the offer comes first, the reply (after the new וַיֹּאמְרוּ) second.

commentary.summary: Rashi: in the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings, bread is 'the support of the heart': 'sustain your hearts' here, 'sustain your heart with a morsel of bread' (Judg. 19:5), 'bread that sustains the heart of man' (Ps. 104:15). R. Hama: the text writes לִבְּכֶם, not לְבַבְכֶם (with two bets, the two inclinations), which shows that the evil inclination does not rule over angels. The English follows the plain sense.
Rashi: 'afterward you may go on' means afterwards you may go on your way. The English follows this.
Rashi: 'I ask this of you, since you have passed by me to honour me.' The English 'since you have passed by your servant' follows the reason clause.
Rashi: ki al-ken means 'like al asher', 'on account of which', as in Gen. 19:8, 33:10, 38:26 and Num. 10:31. The English renders it 'since'.
Ibn Ezra: 'since you have passed', as our predecessors said: the phrase equals 'since' (hu'il), as in 'for this they came' (19:8). The English 'since' follows.

Ibn Ezra: 'Do so, as you have said' is a way of courtesy (derekh musar): 'a morsel of bread is enough'. The visitors answer in the same modest tone as Abraham's offer. The English keeps their reply as agreement.

context: 'A morsel of bread' is courteous understatement: the meal that follows (18:6–8) is lavish. The Hebrew idiom for refreshing oneself with food is 'sustain the heart'; in Hebrew thought the heart (לֵב) is the seat of mind, will and appetite as well as feeling.

segments.english: Abraham hurried to the tent, to Sarah, and said, "Hurry! Three seahs of fine flour: knead it and make cakes."
segments.literal: and-hurried Abraham to-the-tent to Sarah and-said hurry three seahs flour fine-flour knead and-make cakes

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of the piel: 'hasten, make haste'.
directional he: 'to the tent'.
wayyiqtol, 3ms.
piel imperative, 2fs: addressed to Sarah.
the numeral is feminine to agree with seahs.
a dry measure; the unit is not converted.

qemaḥ, ground meal. With סֹלֶת it is 'meal, fine flour': three seahs of fine wheat meal. Rashi: two things, qemaḥ (for the cooks' starch) and solet (for the cakes). Ramban (plain sense) and Radak: meal from which the fine flour is made.
solet, the fine flour for the cakes.
imperative, 2fs.
imperative, 2fs, with the conjunction.
plural of 'ugah, a flat cake.

phrases.literal: 'and-hurried Abraham'.
'to-the-tent to Sarah': the directional ending and the preposition.
'and-said'.
'hurry': the piel imperative, feminine, addressed to Sarah.
'three seahs meal fine-flour': the two nouns in apposition, 'meal, fine flour'; Rashi reads two ingredients.
'knead and-make cakes': two feminine singular imperatives; the object of 'knead' is the flour.

grammar: The imperatives מַהֲרִי, לוּשִׁי and עֲשִׂי are feminine singular, addressed to Sarah.
The numeral 'three' (שְׁלֹשׁ) is feminine to agree with the feminine noun סְאָה (plural סְאִים).
קֶמַח סֹלֶת: the two nouns stand together, 'meal, fine flour'; 'to the tent' ends in the directional הָ- (הָאֹהֱלָה), and the preposition אֶל introduces Sarah.

commentary.summary: Rashi: solet (fine flour) is for the cakes, while qemah (flour) is the cooks' starch, used to cover the pot to draw off the scum. The English keeps flour as an ingredient beside the fine flour; Rashi's reading is recorded here.
Ibn Ezra gives only a parallel for the form: לוּשִׁי 'is like וַתֵּלֶשׁ' (ותלש). He does not change the sense; the English keeps 'knead'.

Ramban, on the plain sense: 'three seahs of meal to make solet from them'; she took from the three seahs a little clean fine flour. He also reports the Midrash (three seahs for each guest) and Rashi's two things and asks why so much bread for three men. The English reads one batch of fine flour.

context: A seah is a dry measure, a third of an ephah. Its modern value is uncertain; estimates run from about seven to more than ten litres. Three seahs is a very large quantity for three guests; the commentators explain it as lavish hospitality or as food for the household.
סֹלֶת is fine wheat flour, a luxury; עֻגוֹת are round flat loaves baked quickly on hot stones or in embers (compare 1 Kgs 19:6). Kneading and baking were the work of the women of the household.

segments.english: Abraham ran to the herd and took a young bull, tender and good, and gave it to the young servant, and hurried to prepare it.
segments.literal: and-to the-herd ran Abraham and-took son-of herd tender and-good and-gave to the-lad and-hurried to-prepare it

tokens.note: qatal, 3ms, fronted: the Hebrew puts the place first.
wayyiqtol, 3ms.
construct: 'son of the herd', a young bull.
the noun 'herd, cattle' in the absolute.
adjective, masculine singular.
adjective, masculine singular: 'good' in the sense of 'excellent'. Radak reads 'good' as 'fat' (not adopted).
wayyiqtol, 3ms.
the young attendant of the household. Radak: הַמְשָׁרֵת, 'the servant' (sense 2). Rashi: Ishmael, whom Abraham trained in the commandments (a midrash).
wayyiqtol of the piel.
infinitive construct.
the object marker with the 3ms suffix.

phrases.literal: 'to-the-herd ran Abraham': the Hebrew puts the place first; the English puts the subject first.

phrases.english: and took a young bull, tender and good
phrases.literal: 'and-took son-of herd tender and-good'.

phrases.english: and gave it to the young servant
phrases.literal: 'and-gave to the-lad': the object is the bull, unstated in the Hebrew.
'and-hurried to-prepare it'.

grammar: The sentence begins with the fronted prepositional phrase 'to the herd'; the verb ran (qatal) follows, then a chain of wayyiqtols.
Ben bakar is a construct: 'son of the herd', the idiom for a young bull. The adjectives tender and good are masculine singular, agreeing with it.
The infinitive construct with the object marker (la-'asot oto) gives 'to prepare it'.
The accents: the tipha on 'hurried' (18:7.13) marks the last clause; the silluq comes at the end of the verse.
segments.note: Rashi's midrash is that there were three bulls, so that the three guests could be fed three tongues in mustard (Bava Metzia 87a). The Hebrew is singular (בֶּן־בָּקָר), and Radak reads a single small male, so the English keeps 'a young bull' and the reading is recorded in the commentary. The subject of וַיְמַהֵר is not marked: Radak takes it as Abraham's zeal; the servant is also possible.

commentary.summary: Rashi: there were three young bulls, so that the three guests could be fed three tongues in mustard (Bava Metzia 87a). The Hebrew is singular, so the English does not adopt this; it is a midrash on the quantity.
Rashi: 'the lad' is Ishmael, whom Abraham trained in the commandments (Bereshit Rabba). The English keeps 'the lad' without the identification; Radak reads 'the servant'.
Radak: 'to the lad' means to the servant; the midrash says Ishmael. The English follows the plain sense, 'the young servant'.

context: Meat was a rare luxury for a household of herders, who lived mostly on milk, curds and bread; slaughtering a choice young animal for a guest marks great honour (compare 1 Sam. 28:24).
Abraham's household includes many servants (14:14, 17:23), one of whom prepares the animal.

segments.english: He took curds and milk and the young bull which he had prepared, and set them before them, and he stood by them under the tree, and they ate.
segments.literal: and-took curds and-milk and-son-of the-herd which he-made and-set before-them and-he standing upon-them under the-tree and-they-ate

tokens.note: wayyiqtol, 3ms.
ḥem'ah. The entry gives 'curd'; the exact food (curds, soured or clotted milk, or butter) is uncertain. Rashi: the fat skimmed from the surface of milk.

phrases.literal: 'and-took cream'.

phrases.english: and milk and the young bull which he had prepared
phrases.literal: 'and-milk and-son-of the-bull which made': the relative clause gives the bull Abraham had prepared.
'and-set before-them': the object 'them' is the food; 'before them' the men.

phrases.english: and he stood by them under the tree
phrases.literal: 'and-he standing upon-them under the-tree'.
'and-ate': the plain verb; Rashi's 'appeared to eat' is recorded in the commentary.

grammar: The chain of wayyiqtols (he took, he set, they ate) carries the meal forward; 'and he stood' is a circumstantial clause in the middle (a waw, the pronoun and a participle).
The relative clause 'which he had prepared' (אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה) is a qatal that precedes the setting-out; Radak adds 'through the servant'.

The Hebrew names no bread; Radak supposes bread was served first, as 18:6 implies, and the verse lists only the further dishes. Rashi has a midrash (Sarah's niddah) for the omission. The English names no bread.
The etnaḥta on לִפְנֵיהֶם divides the verse: the serving comes first, the standing and the eating second.
segments.note: Ibn Ezra (comment on 18:8, filed at 18:1): וַיֹּאכֵלוּ means 'the bread was consumed', as in 'which the fire consumes' (Lev. 6:3), that is, he does not take it that the visitors ate as men do. The English keeps 'they ate': the narrative sets the food before them and Lot's visitors also 'eat' (19:3), and the reading of Ibn Ezra rests on a view of what angels are, not on the Hebrew grammar of the verse (the subject is plural and active). The reading is recorded in the apparatus and the commentary. Rashi's 'appeared to eat' is also recorded.

commentary.summary: Rashi: no bread is mentioned because Sarah's period began that day, which made the dough unclean (Bava Metzia 86b). A midrash on the omission. Radak holds that bread was certainly served first (18:6) and the verse lists only the further dishes. The English names no bread because the Hebrew names none.
Rashi: חֶמְאָה is the fat of the milk, skimmed from its surface. The English 'curds' follows BDB; Rashi's 'milk fat' is recorded as a nearby reading.

Rashi: אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה means 'which he had prepared'; each portion as it was prepared he brought and set before them (Aramaic: kama kama, 'first by first'). The English 'which he had prepared' follows the gloss.

Rashi: 'and they ate' means they appeared to eat, and from this one learns not to depart from the custom of the house (Bava Metzia 87a). The English keeps 'they ate'. Ibn Ezra, on 18:1, reads the verb as 'the bread was consumed'; the two comments differ.

Radak: the verse names only milk-foods and meat so that they may eat from whichever they choose; bread need not be mentioned, since bread would have been put before even the lowest guest first (and 18:6 shows he had it made). The English names no bread.

apparatus: Ibn Ezra: ויאכלו = 'the bread was consumed' (compare Lev. 6:3), not that the visitors ate. Not adopted; the active plural verb is read as the plain sense (question for the editor, since Ibn Ezra is normative).
Rashi (Bava Metzia 87a): they appeared to eat. Ramban cites the rabbis (Genesis Rabbah): each visitor in turn departed as the meal went on. Radak: the whole scene is a prophetic vision.
context: חֶמְאָה is a milk product; the exact food is uncertain (curds, soured or clotted milk, or butter). Cow's milk and meat are served together: the later rabbinic separation of milk and meat is not in this narrative and is not read into it.
A host who stands by his guests while they eat attends on them; it shows deference, not distance.
